To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the analytical method used for the detection of CW agents must be able to detect the entire range of chemical warfare agents and precursors and their simulants and must provide a high degree of accuracy, precision, and selectivity for the identification of these agents and their simulants.

(1) a modern, mobile laboratory, equipped with a gas chromatography/mass spectrometer (GC/MS) and a GC with an IMS detector, can provide the required analytical information on-site; (2) the GC/MS can be operated in a fully automated mode and provide high-quality data; and (3) the GC/IMS can operate in a fully automated, unattended mode for 24 hours and provide data on-site.
the use of GC/MS or IMS/MS is recommended for the detection of CW agents in the field.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new, sensitive and selective sensors for the detection and monitoring of chemical warfare agents and related compounds in the environment.

the development of new analytical methods for the detection and determination of chemical warfare agents and toxic industrial chemicals, which are based on the principles of gas chromatography, ion mobility spectrometric and electrochemical detection.
development of new, highly sensitive and selective sensors and analytical methods for the rapid detection of CW agents, their precursors, and degradation products.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the best analytical method for the verification of the destruction of CW agents is a mobile laboratory that is capable of performing high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), capillary electrophoresis (CE), and gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) analysis.

there is no analytical method that can be used for on-site verification of CW agent destruction that is capable of providing all the information required by the CWC, and that the most appropriate analytical methods for on-site verification are those that are simple and provide two-dimensional analytical information.
the best approach for on-site chemical agent identification is the combination of two- and three-dimensional methods, such as the combination of GC/IMS or GC/mass spectrometry (MS).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CWC is an excellent international agreement and that it has the potential to be an even greater success than the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC).

we are in favor of a two-dimensional analytical method for the detection of CW agents, such as GC/IMS, and we are against a single dimension analytical method, such as IMS, as the only analytical method for the on-site detection of CW agents.
we have developed and validated a new method for the detection and determination of chemical warfare agents and their simulants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single analytical method that can provide a full range of data for all possible CW agents and precursors.

the CWC is not a treaty against chemical weapons, but a treaty against the production, stockpiling, and use of chemical weapons, as well as against the proliferation of chemical weapons and their precursors.
a single analytical method cannot be used to detect all possible chemical warfare agents.
